result:
There is a particular kind of magic in finding a stranger’s handwritten list. It can be a scrap of paper on a bus seat, a receipt with a few words scribbled on the back, or a crumpled page in a library book. The list might read:

*avocados  
*oat milk  
*call mom  
*return red sweater*

And just like that, a life opens.

I have a shoebox of these. Some are grocery lists. Some are to-do lists. One is a list of songs someone wanted to remember, in handwriting so neat it looks printed. Another is a list of apologies, never sent, perhaps never meant to be read by anyone but the writer. The paper is soft from folding and unfolding.

Why do I keep them? I think because they are the opposite of everything loud and performed. They were never meant for an audience. They are pure, unsanitized thought—captured in the moment before a person crossed an item off, or added one at the last minute, or tore the paper in frustration.

We are all making lists, in a way. Not just on paper, but in our heads: things to do, people to love, dreams to guard. We check them off as the year passes. Some items get crossed out and never spoken of again. Some get rewritten onto a new list, carried over, stubborn.

The best part of finding a list is the imagining. Who is this person? Were the avocados for a celebratory dinner or a lonely Tuesday? Did they ever call mom? Did they return the sweater, or did it sit in the closet until it became a curtain in a story they told at parties? I will never know. The list is a door left open, and I am not allowed to step inside. That is exactly what makes it beautiful.

So I keep collecting. It is my quiet rebellion against a world that always wants us to move faster, post more, perform better. A list is a pause. It is someone saying: *This is what matters today. This is what I will do, or try, or hope to remember.*

Maybe that is all any of us are doing.

In the meantime, I’ll keep an eye out for the next scrap, and I’ll add my own line to my list: *write freely, more often.*
